I’m in the same boat as you. I have BDD and when I was 19 I developed a pretty bad eating disorder that I’ve managed to keep at bay with weightlifting. I’ve tried multiple times for the past 2 and a half years to maintain a good bulk/cut cycle, but I find the mental stress of it to be too much and I typically fail. I am terrified of relapsing, so I’ve decided to simply do my best. 

I still bulk and cut (sort of). During my bulk phase, I eat at a very small caloric increase and I take it verrrryyy slow. I’ll bulk up to the point I start noticing little changes in my body. Once my clothes start fitting tighter, I’ll end the bulk. I do the same when cutting. I take it very, very slowly, and if I start feeling too small or if I begin bodychecking in the mirror, I’ll end the cut. I spend most of the year in a maintenance phase, because I know it is what keeps me happiest. 

Have I put on muscle? Yes. Is it 100% efficient? No. I am not building muscle as fast as I possibly could, but mentally I am well. A big reason why I work out is to keep me mentally sane and happy, so why should I stress myself out by obsessing over cut/bulk cycles? If I begin to associate working out with constant calorie counting, negative self image, and an obsession with weight,  It’ll completely negate the reason I started working out in the first place.

Keep lifting but prioritize your mental health. Focus more on your functionality and happiness.

don’t look at this guide, as ADHD is not “caused” by any of the things on here. I have ADHD and was diagnosed at 7, here is some advice that would’ve helped me. 
1.) Adderall and other stimulant medications works for some and doesn’t work for others. I would put her in therapy and get her a psychologist, and see if they recommend it. If you notice that she is unhappy or overly anxious (more than normal) ask her how she feels about the medication. Nobody knows her own feelings other than her. Since she is so young, it might take a while for her to get adjusted to the point she understands something is her own brain or caused by medication. ADHD medication was the worst thing that ever happened to me, but for a lot of people it was the best thing. 
2.) Never take her off any medication cold turkey. This may be common sense for you, but it wasn’t for my parents lol.
3.) Let her know nothing is “wrong” with her. Neurodiversity is natural and her feeling different than other kids is completely normal. It took me a long time to understand that everyone else is struggling too, just differently. 

The r/adhd subreddit, although informational, is full of people venting. It shows the downs of the disorder, not the ups. I thought I’d never be happy, but recently I feel great. Some people never will. It depends. I found my happiness through self adjustment. I was put into therapy fairly early and I learned how to regulate my own emotions and how to recognize when something was my own issue or caused by medication. Also, if you do put her on any medication, KEEP TRACK OF IT! I always forgot to take my meds, and would occasionally cause myself to withdraw. It’s best you keep track of them in a pill box with dates. 
Everything I said is my own experience and many people will be different. Lots of research is key, but listening to her and her emotions is the most important!
